questions.q: Meenal reads the Aikyamatya Sūktam verse and tells her class, 'Early Indian kings ruled entirely on their own.' Which statement from the chapter best answers her?
questions.a: Kings worked in consultation with assemblies, ministers and officers. The chapter says the king was not an independent ruler. The secret ballot is a modern device, and the other two options are not in the chapter.
o: Kings worked in consultation with assemblies, ministers and officers
Kings were chosen by a secret ballot of all adults in the kingdom
Kings consulted only foreign travellers before taking a decision
Kings let the Sabha and Samiti meet but never heard their views

questions.q: A class debate says, 'Democracy came to India only because the British ruled it.' Which line from the chapter weakens this claim most?
questions.a: Foreign rule limited participation, and the freedom struggle revived democratic ideas. The chapter says colonial rule altered political structures and limited participation, and that the struggle for independence revived democratic ideas that already had roots in Sabha, Samiti and the Saṁghas.
o: Foreign rule limited participation, and the freedom struggle revived democratic ideas
British rule gave Indians their first experience of choosing leaders by voting
Foreign rule strengthened local assemblies by bringing them under one king
Democratic ideas reached India only through the Constituent Assembly's Debates

questions.q: In 2040 Parliament wishes to change a provision of the Constitution to meet new social needs, without giving up its basic values. What route does the chapter say is open?
questions.a: A lawful amendment under Article 368. The chapter says the Assembly wanted a dynamic document that can evolve through lawful amendments under Article 368 without compromising its fundamental values.
o: A lawful amendment under Article 368
A fresh Constituent Assembly rewriting the whole text
A single court order under Article 32
A show of hands in every Gram Sabha

questions.q:
Read the statements about democratic roots and the Constitution.
1. In early times Indian kings ruled as independent rulers who did not consult assemblies.
2. Members of the Bauddha Saṁghas could choose their leader and decide matters by voting.
3. The Constitution provides for amendments under Article 368 so that it stays responsive to changing needs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: the chapter says the king worked in consultation with assemblies, ministers and officers. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution of India was meant to be a dynamic document, not a rigid legal code.
Reason (R): The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to draft it.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are stated in the chapter. But the length of time taken does not explain why the framers wanted a flexible text; the reason is their belief in lawful amendment under Article 368.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation with the early Indian practice it resembles, as described in the chapter.
1. Members of a monastic order debate a question and vote to choose their head
2. A verse calls for one counsel, one assembly and one mind
3. A ruler takes a decision only after hearing assemblies and ministers
4. A group is asked to amend a law under Article 368 without losing its basic values
a. Collective thinking and unity of purpose in the Aikyamatya Sūktam
b. The Bauddha Saṁgha
c. Flexibility through lawful amendment
d. The king working with assemblies, ministers and officers
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c. Saṁgha: debate and voting; the verse: unity of purpose; the king: consulting assemblies, ministers and officers; Article 368: lawful amendment.

questions.q: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The gap between the two dates is ___ days.
India had over 96.8 crore registered voters in 2024 against a population of over 140 crore. Taking 140 crore, voters were about ___ per cent of the population (nearest whole number).
True or False: The chapter says that democratic ideas appeared in India suddenly when the Constitution came into force in 1950.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the democratic ethos did not emerge suddenly but evolved through a long historical process, from Vedic assemblies and the Saṁghas to the freedom struggle and the Constituent Assembly.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: democratic ethos grew over a long historical process, with roots in early assemblies

questions.q: (a) Name the two early institutions or communities the chapter uses to show that collective decision-making is old in India. (b) Choose one and say how it kept power from resting with a single person.
questions.a: (a) The Vedic assemblies (Sabha, Samiti, Vidhata) and the Bauddha Saṁghas; the early republican gaṇas are also mentioned. (b) In the Saṁgha, members could choose their leader and decide by voting; in the Vedic period the king worked in consultation with assemblies, ministers and officers.
s: (a) Two valid examples from the chapter
(b) A specific way the chosen one shared decision-making power

questions.q: (a) The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. Express the complete years and months part in months. (b) Why did its members build in Article 368 instead of treating the text as a rigid legal code?
questions.a: (a) 2 years 11 months = 2 x 12 + 11 = 35 months (plus 18 days). (b) The Constituent Assembly's Debates reflect a belief that the Constitution should be a dynamic document that can evolve through lawful amendments without compromising its fundamental values, staying responsive to changing socio-political needs.
s: (a) 35 months, with the 18 days left over
(b) Flexibility through lawful amendment while keeping fundamental values

questions.q: Differentiate between a country that only holds elections and a democracy as the chapter describes it. Give one thing the second has that the first may lack.
questions.a: The chapter calls democracy a system of self-governance with institutions, rules and practices that let people take part in decision-making at local, state and national levels; it is not limited to elections. The second has these participatory practices, for example Gram Sabhas, a free media or rule of law, which a mere election-holding state may lack.
s: Democracy is wider than elections: institutions, rules and practices of participation
One feature beyond elections named correctly

questions.q: The chapter says the Constitution ensures that no citizen is discriminated against. A school notice says, 'Admission will not depend on a child's caste or place of birth.' List two other grounds from the chapter that such a notice should also name.
questions.a: Religion, race and sex (any two). The chapter lists religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth.
s: Two further grounds correctly chosen

questions.q: Rohit claims: 'The framers wanted a Constitution that could never be changed, so that its values would stay pure.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No, the claim does not hold. The Constituent Assembly's Debates show a belief that the Constitution should not be a rigid legal code but a dynamic document able to evolve through lawful amendments. Article 368 provides for amendments. The values stay fixed; the text can be amended without compromising them.
s: Verdict: the claim is not correct
Evidence: the framers wanted a dynamic document, not a rigid code
Article 368 and the idea of amending without giving up fundamental values

questions.q: Write a short school-election situation in which a class both talks things over and then votes, so that it echoes both the Aikyamatya Sūktam and the Bauddha Saṁgha. Name the feature each part echoes.
questions.a: Any valid situation, for example: the class discusses three options for the annual-day theme until everyone has spoken (shared discussion and unity of purpose, as in the verse), then votes to choose the class leader or theme (decision by voting, as in the Saṁgha).
s: A believable situation with discussion and a vote
Discussion linked to collective thinking or unity of purpose
Voting linked to the Bauddha Saṁgha

questions.q: Interpret why foreign rule 'limited people's participation' in governance but the long struggle for independence 'revived and strengthened' democratic ideas. Give two reasons.
questions.a: Foreign rule altered political structures, so people had little share in governing themselves. The struggle was a demand to govern themselves, so it brought back values of consultation and shared responsibility that were already part of India's tradition, and it prepared the ground for the Constituent Assembly formed in 1946.
s: Why foreign rule limited participation
Why the struggle for self-rule revived democratic ideas
A link to the Constituent Assembly or older traditions

questions.q: The chapter says the democratic ethos 'did not emerge suddenly'. Justify this with five stages in order: Vedic assemblies, the Aikyamatya verse, the Bauddha Saṁghas, colonial rule and the freedom struggle, and the Constituent Assembly.
questions.a: Vedic Sabha, Samiti and Vidhata involved collective decision-making and the king consulted assemblies, ministers and officers. The Rigveda verse values shared discussion, consensus and unity of purpose. The Saṁghas encouraged debate and let members choose their leader and decide by voting. Colonial rule limited participation, but the struggle for independence revived democratic ideas. The Constituent Assembly formed in 1946 drew on indigenous traditions and global democratic values to draft the Constitution in 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. Together these show a long evolution.
s: Vedic assemblies and consultation
The verse's collective thinking and unity of purpose
The Saṁghas' debate and voting
Colonial limits and the revival through the freedom struggle
The Constituent Assembly of 1946 drawing on both Indian and global values

questions.q: Compare the evidence of the Aikyamatya Sūktam verse and of the Bauddha Saṁghas for India's democratic traditions. Say which shows decision-making by voting more directly, and then evaluate why Article 368 matters to keeping a Constitution democratic over time.
questions.a: The verse shows values of shared discussion, consensus and unity of purpose but does not describe voting. The Saṁghas encouraged debate, and members could choose their leader and decide through voting, so they show voting more directly. Article 368 matters because it lets the Constitution evolve through lawful amendment without compromising fundamental values; a rigid text could not answer changing socio-political needs, and citizens might have to look outside it for change.
s: What the verse shows: consultation and unity, not voting
What the Saṁghas show: debate, choosing the leader, voting
Verdict: Saṁghas are the more direct evidence of voting
What Article 368 allows
Why that keeps a Constitution responsive and democratic

questions.q:
Class 9's Student Samiti at a Nagpur school has 40 members and must choose the Annual Day theme. One group wants to keep discussing until everyone agrees; this took three meetings of 45 minutes each last year. The other wants a vote in a single 45-minute meeting. A trial vote today gives 22 for 'Water Heroes' and 18 for 'Our Heritage'.
(a) Which early Indian practice does the first group's method resemble, and which does the second group's resemble? Name one for each.
(b) Work out how many minutes the first method needs, and whether 22 votes is a majority of the 40 members.
(c) The Samiti may adopt only one method this year. Which would you choose, and what does your choice give up?
questions.a: (a) Discussion until agreement resembles the Aikyamatya Sūktam's collective thinking and unity of purpose (Vedic assemblies); voting resembles the Bauddha Saṁgha. (b) 3 x 45 = 135 minutes; 22 of 40 is 55 per cent, more than half, so a majority. (c) Either with a reasoned trade-off: consensus builds unity but costs 90 more minutes; voting is quick and the 22-18 majority is clear but leaves 18 members unconvinced.
s: (a) Consensus linked to the verse or assemblies, voting linked to the Saṁgha
(b) 135 minutes and 22 of 40 is a majority (55 per cent)
(c) A choice with the benefit and the cost stated using the data

questions.q:
A museum is setting up a corridor wall on India's democratic roots. It has three panels. Panel P shows a monastic community whose members chose a leader and decided by voting. Panel Q shows an assembly formed in 1946 that took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to draft a text. Panel R shows a verse that speaks of one assembly and one mind. The wall has room for only two of the three panels.
(a) Name what each of P, Q and R shows, using the chapter.
(b) Panel Q's text allows lawful change under one Article. Name it and say what the framers wanted the document to be.
(c) Which two panels would you keep for students, and what story of democracy is lost by dropping the third?
questions.a: (a) P: the Bauddha Saṁgha; Q: the Constituent Assembly; R: the Aikyamatya Sūktam of the Rigveda. (b) Article 368; a dynamic document able to evolve through lawful amendments without compromising its fundamental values. (c) Either defensible choice with the cost stated: dropping R loses the idea of consensus and unity of purpose; dropping P loses a working example of voting; dropping Q loses how those ideas became written law.
s: (a) Three correct identifications
(b) Article 368 and the dynamic-document idea
(c) Two panels chosen, with the lost part of the story named

questions.q: A magistrate's nephew and a vegetable seller are both caught breaking the same traffic rule. The officer fines both equally and does not let the nephew off. Which principle does this show?
questions.a: Rule of law, since no one is above the law. The chapter says the Rule of Law establishes equality before the law and that no one is above the law. The other three are real principles but do not apply to this situation.
o: Rule of law, since no one is above the law
Popular sovereignty, since power lies with the people
Universal adult franchise, since all can vote in secret
Separation of powers, since the judiciary makes the laws

questions.q: In a hostel election, some older students pressure a 19-year-old to show them how she voted. Which feature of the franchise described in the chapter protects her?
questions.a: Every citizen of 18 years and above votes through a secret ballot. The chapter defines Universal Adult Franchise as the right of every citizen aged 18 and above to vote through a secret ballot.
o: Every citizen of 18 years and above votes through a secret ballot
Only heads of families may cast a vote on behalf of others
A vote is open so that the elected can see who backed them
Only citizens aged 21 and above are allowed to vote in person

questions.q: A journalist is detained and her family says the law was not followed. According to the chapter, which step is open to her to protect her fundamental rights?
questions.a: Seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226. The chapter says citizens can seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226, and that Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts of law.
o: Seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226
Wait for Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368
Ask the Election Commission to cancel the detention order
Accept it, because Fundamental Rights cannot be enforced in courts

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Fundamental Rights.
1. Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts of law, subject to reasonable restrictions in accordance with the procedure established by law.
2. The Right to Freedom of Religion is placed in Articles 19-22.
3. Article 21A, added in 2009, provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: Articles 19-22 are the Right to Freedom, while the Right to Freedom of Religion is in Articles 25-28.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The rule of law protects citizens against arbitrary action by those in power.
Reason (R): No citizen can be punished without following the procedure established by law, and everyone gets a fair opportunity to defend their rights.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are stated in the chapter, and the reason explains the assertion: a fixed procedure and a chance to defend oneself are exactly what stop arbitrary action.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Counting both end Articles, the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18) spans ___ Articles.
Adding the Articles in all six ranges the chapter names for Fundamental Rights (14-18, 19-22, 23-24, 25-28, 29-30 and 32), the total is ___ Articles.
A newly elected sarpanch tells villagers, 'My authority is mine by birth, not by your vote.' Which principle from the chapter does this statement contradict?
questions.a: Popular sovereignty, because the state derives its authority from the people. The chapter says that in a democracy the ultimate source of power lies with the people and the state derives its authority from them.
o: Popular sovereignty, because the state derives its authority from the people
Rule of law, because courts must hear all complaints in public
Separation of powers, because she is acting as a judge
Procedure established by law, because it is found only in Article 14

questions.q: True or False: According to the chapter, Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts of law, and a citizen whose right is violated can seek remedy under Articles 32 and 226.
questions.a: True. The chapter says any violation can lead to legal action, that citizens can seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226, and that these rights are enforceable in courts of law.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rights are enforceable in courts, with remedies under Articles 32 and 226

questions.q: (a) Which two Articles does the chapter name for seeking constitutional remedies? (b) The chapter calls Fundamental Rights 'indivisible and inalienable'. What does that tell a student about whether a government can simply take a right away?
questions.a: (a) Articles 32 and 226. (b) Inalienable means the right belongs to the person and cannot be taken away at will; the only limits are reasonable restrictions in accordance with the procedure established by law.
s: (a) Articles 32 and 226
(b) Rights cannot be taken away at will; only reasonable restrictions by due procedure

questions.q: A village has 640 residents, of whom 150 are below 18. Assume all are citizens. (a) How many can vote under Universal Adult Franchise? (b) Why does the chapter attach the word 'secret' to the ballot?
questions.a: (a) 640 - 150 = 490 voters. (b) So that each voter can choose freely, without being pressed by others; the chapter says every citizen aged 18 and above votes through a secret ballot, which supports popular sovereignty.
s: (a) 490 eligible voters
(b) Secret ballot lets a citizen choose freely, which supports popular sovereignty

questions.q: Differentiate between 'equality before law' and 'equal protection of law' using the chapter's own descriptions, with one example for each.
questions.a: Equality before law: every individual, irrespective of status, identity or rank, is treated equally by the law, e.g. a minister and a clerk face the same court. Equal protection of law: all persons in similar circumstances are treated equally without arbitrary discrimination, e.g. two shopkeepers charged with the same offence get the same treatment.
s: Equality before law: no one's rank or status matters, with an example
Equal protection: similar circumstances, similar treatment, with an example

questions.q: Article 21A, added in 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14. A family has a 5-year-old, a 12-year-old and a 16-year-old. (a) Which child does the Article cover? (b) Why does the chapter call this Article significant for democracy?
questions.a: (a) The 12-year-old, because the Article covers ages 6 to 14. (b) The chapter lists it for discussion of its significance; education lets citizens understand and use their rights and take part in decision-making, which a democracy needs.
s: (a) The 12-year-old only
(b) A reasoned link between education and informed participation

questions.q: Tara says, 'Fundamental Rights are enforceable and inalienable, so no restriction can ever be placed on them.' Test her statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does say these rights are enforceable in courts of law, indivisible and inalienable. But it adds that they are subject to reasonable restrictions in accordance with the procedure established by law, so 'no restriction ever' is wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: enforceable and inalienable
The wrong part: reasonable restrictions by procedure established by law are allowed

questions.q: Show that the rule of law cannot exist in a town where disputes are settled by force or personal influence. Use the chapter's description of the rule of law.
questions.a: The chapter says that under the rule of law disputes are resolved in a court of law through procedures established by law, not by force or personal influence. If influence or force decides, then some people are above the law, equal protection is lost, and misuse of power is not prevented. So the rule of law cannot exist there.
s: Rule of law means disputes go to courts by established procedure
Force or influence puts someone above the law and breaks equality
Conclusion: misuse of power is unchecked, so the rule of law is absent

questions.q: Interpret how Universal Adult Franchise and popular sovereignty are connected. Give two reasons and an example from your ward or village.
questions.a: Popular sovereignty means the state's authority comes from the people. Universal Adult Franchise lets every citizen aged 18 and above vote by secret ballot, so (i) the people choose who forms the government and makes policies, and (ii) a government elected through free and fair elections draws its authority from them. Example: electing a ward member.
s: Popular sovereignty: authority comes from the people
Franchise as the way people exercise it, with two reasons
A valid local example

questions.q: List the six Fundamental Rights with their Articles. Then work out which right spans the most Articles and by how many it exceeds the right placed in Articles 23-24, and explain why the Right to Constitutional Remedies is needed for the others.
questions.a: Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against Exploitation (23-24), Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32). Equality spans 5 Articles, the most; Articles 23-24 span 2, so Equality exceeds it by 3. Article 32 (and Article 226) lets citizens go to court when a right is violated, so the other rights can be enforced.
s: All six rights named
Equality identified as the largest span, with 5 - 2 = 3
Article 32 and 226 named as the remedy
Why enforcement is needed for the other rights

questions.q: A district official orders a shopkeeper to be jailed for a month without telling him of any charge or allowing him to be heard, saying 'the order is mine'. Analyse the order using three ideas from the chapter: the rule of law, procedure established by law, and the remedies open to the shopkeeper.
questions.a: The rule of law means no one is above the law, and disputes are resolved by courts through procedure established by law, not personal influence; 'the order is mine' puts the official above the law. Article 21 says no person is deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law, and the chapter says no citizen can be punished without it and everyone gets a fair chance to defend themselves. The shopkeeper can seek constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226, because Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts.
s: Rule of law: no one above the law, order by personal authority fails
Procedure established by law and Article 21
Fair opportunity to defend denied
Remedies under Articles 32 and 226

questions.q:
Ward 7 of Nandgaon has 1,250 citizens, of whom 275 are below 18. In the municipal poll held by secret ballot, 780 votes were cast. Candidate Sunita won 429 votes. She says, 'I speak for the whole ward.' A retired teacher replies that many did not support her.
(a) How many people in the ward were eligible to vote?
(b) What was the turnout among eligible voters, and what share of the votes cast did Sunita win?
(c) Is Sunita's claim to speak for the whole ward justified? Give a decision using the figures and the idea of popular sovereignty, and name one thing that would make the ward's voice stronger.
questions.a: (a) 1,250 - 275 = 975 eligible. (b) Turnout 780/975 = 80 per cent; Sunita 429/780 = 55 per cent of votes cast. (c) Either view with figures: she has a majority of those who voted, which is how the people's authority is used; but she has only 429/975 = 44 per cent of eligible voters, so the ward's voice is incomplete. Higher turnout would strengthen it.
s: (a) 975 eligible voters, using the age of 18
(b) 80 per cent turnout and 55 per cent of votes
(c) Decision backed by 55 per cent against 44 per cent, with a way to improve participation

questions.q:
A town council bans all public meetings in the market area for 7 days, because a festival of 40,000 visitors is expected. A group of residents who wished to hold a peaceful meeting on a public matter says its freedom is being taken away. The council says the ban is temporary and was issued by following the proper procedure.
(a) Under which of the six Fundamental Rights, with which Articles, would the residents' claim to speak and meet fall?
(b) Where may the group go if it believes its right is violated, and why can a court hear it?
(c) Should the court accept the ban as a reasonable restriction? Take a position and name the fact from the chapter that supports it and one risk that remains.
questions.a: (a) The Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22). (b) The courts, through constitutional remedies under Articles 32 and 226, because Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts of law. (c) Either position is defensible. The ban can be upheld because the chapter says rights are subject to reasonable restrictions in accordance with procedure established by law and 7 days is a small part of the year (about 1.9 per cent); or the ban can be set aside as too wide if it covers all meetings. The risk: restrictions can drift into permanent silencing of citizens.
s: (a) Right to Freedom, Articles 19-22
(b) Courts under Articles 32 and 226, rights enforceable in courts
(c) A reasoned position using reasonable restrictions and procedure, with a risk

questions.q: In a state, the same group of legislators passes a rule, orders its enforcement and also sits as the judges who punish those who break it. Which danger does the chapter say the separation of powers is meant to prevent?
questions.a: Concentration of power in a single organ of government. The chapter says the legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary interprets them, so that power is not concentrated in any one organ.
o: Concentration of power in a single organ of government
Competition among several political parties for votes
Review of an amendment by the judiciary after it is passed
Citizens asking for records held by public authorities

questions.q: Ismail wants to know how a district office spent Rs 12 lakh on a village road. Which law does the chapter name as letting citizens seek such information from government agencies?
questions.a: The Right to Information Act, 2005. The chapter names the RTI Act, 2005. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 is the framework within which parties function, PESA relates to Gram Sabhas, and Article 46 concerns weaker sections.
o: The Right to Information Act, 2005
The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The PESA Act (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas), 1996
Article 46 of the Constitution

questions.q: An assembly has 230 seats. Party X wins 112 seats and Party Y wins 14. If they form a coalition, can they form the government under the chapter's rule?
questions.a: Yes, because their 126 seats are more than 50 per cent of 230. More than 50 per cent of 230 means at least 116 seats; the chapter says a party or a coalition securing more than 50 per cent of the seats forms the government.
o: Yes, because their 126 seats are more than 50 per cent of 230
No, because only a single party with over 50 per cent can govern
Yes, because the larger party always forms the government alone
No, because 126 seats are exactly half of the 230 seats

questions.q:
Read the statements about the organs of government and the party system.
1. Parliament can amend the Constitution, and the judiciary can review such amendments to see that they are consistent with its spirit.
2. A party or coalition that secures more than 50 per cent of the seats forms the government, and the largest opposing group becomes the opposition.
3. The judiciary has no power to declare a law unconstitutional, even if it is inconsistent with the constitutional provisions.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says that if a law is inconsistent with the constitutional provisions, the judiciary has the power to declare it unconstitutional.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Checks and balances among the three organs are needed for democratic institutions to function responsibly.
Reason (R): In the chapter's account, the legislature both makes the laws and implements them.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A is true, as the chapter says separation of powers maintains checks and balances. R is false: the legislature makes laws, while the executive implements them.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation with the item from the chapter that it illustrates.
1. A member asks the government about a delayed bridge in the first hour of a parliamentary session
2. A citizen asks a department for details of its spending
3. A court finds a law inconsistent with the Constitution
4. A scheme gives special care to the educational interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
a. The power of the judiciary to declare a law unconstitutional
b. Article 46
c. The Right to Information Act, 2005
d. Question Hour
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b. Question Hour is the first hour of a session when members question the government; the RTI Act enables citizens to seek information; the judiciary can declare a law unconstitutional; Article 46 is about weaker sections.

questions.q: In an assembly of 230 seats, the smallest number of seats that is more than 50 per cent is ___.

A state scheme gives scholarships to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students, saying it promotes their educational and economic interests with special care. Which constitutional provision named in the chapter supports it?
questions.a: Article 46. The chapter quotes Article 46: the State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, in particular the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.
o: Article 46
Article 21A
Article 243(d)
Article 368

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says that the executive's power of enforcement is outside the reach of courts, since it belongs to a separate organ.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the executive power of enforcement agencies is regulated by laws and rules framed by Parliament and can also be reviewed by competent courts.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: enforcement is regulated by Parliament's laws and reviewable by courts

questions.q: (a) Name two institutions that the chapter lists among accountability mechanisms. (b) Which democratic value do they promote, and how can that value build trust between the government and the people?
questions.a: (a) Any two of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the Central Information Commission (CIC), the Lokpal, the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). (b) Transparency; when the government's work is open to scrutiny, citizens can evaluate it, which builds trust.
s: (a) Two correct institutions
(b) Transparency, linked to citizens evaluating the government and trust

questions.q: An assembly has 230 seats and Party A has won 108. (a) How many more seats does it need to form the government? (b) What name does the chapter give to the largest opposing group?
questions.a: (a) More than 50 per cent of 230 is at least 116 seats, so it needs 116 - 108 = 8 more seats (for example from coalition partners). (b) The opposition.
s: (a) 8 more seats, from a threshold of 116
(b) The opposition

questions.q: Differentiate between a Public Interest Litigation and a request under the Right to Information Act in what each does for a citizen.
questions.a: A PIL is a legal action initiated in a court of law to enforce the public interest. A request under the RTI Act asks a government agency for information it holds. One goes to a court for enforcement; the other goes to the department for information.
s: PIL: legal action in a court for public interest
RTI: seeking information from government agencies

questions.q: Explain what 'Question Hour' is and how it helps check the work of a government.
questions.a: Question Hour is the first hour of a parliamentary session when members ask questions to the government. This helps check the government's work and hold it accountable.
s: What Question Hour is
How it holds the government accountable

questions.q: Ravi claims, 'The biggest party always forms the government, even if it has only 40 per cent of the seats, because it is the largest.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that the party or coalition that secures more than 50 per cent of the seats forms the government. A party with 40 per cent must join a coalition to cross 50 per cent; if it cannot, it does not form the government, and the largest opposing group becomes the opposition.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Rule: more than 50 per cent of seats, alone or as a coalition
A 40 per cent party needs partners; it is not enough on its own

questions.q: Think about what would happen if the same organ of government made laws, implemented them and enforced them. Give two consequences, using the chapter's idea of checks and balances.
questions.a: There would be no check on misuse of power: the same body could make a law for its own benefit and apply it without review. Citizens would have no independent body to interpret the law or protect rights. The separation of powers prevents this concentration and maintains checks and balances among the three organs.
s: A consequence: no check on misuse of power
A second consequence: rights unprotected without an independent judiciary
Link to checks and balances and separation of powers

questions.q: The chapter says the government must protect all communities and distribute resources equitably, especially to the most vulnerable. Give three points of explanation, quoting Article 46.
questions.a: Historical factors have led to an unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, so equal treatment alone is not enough. The government must protect communities regardless of caste, gender, religion or region and distribute resources equitably without discrimination. Article 46 says the State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, particularly Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
s: Why: unequal distribution of opportunities due to historical factors
Duty: protect all communities and share resources equitably
Article 46 and its special care for weaker sections

questions.q: Explain how the three organs of government check one another, using three examples from the chapter: the amendment of the Constitution, the enforcement agencies, and a law that conflicts with the Constitution. Then justify why this keeps power from being misused.
questions.a: Parliament can amend the Constitution, but the judiciary can review the amendment to see that it is consistent with the spirit of the Constitution. The executive's enforcement agencies are regulated by laws and rules framed by Parliament and can be reviewed by competent courts. If a law is inconsistent with constitutional provisions, the judiciary can declare it unconstitutional. Because each organ is limited by another, no single organ can act without check, which prevents misuse and protects rights.
s: Amendment by Parliament and its review by the judiciary
Enforcement agencies regulated by Parliament and reviewable by courts
Judiciary declaring an inconsistent law unconstitutional
Roles: legislature makes, executive implements, judiciary interprets
Justification: no single organ is unchecked, so misuse is prevented

questions.q: Evaluate how the multi-party system and the accountability mechanisms in the chapter work together to keep a government answerable to the people. Use the rule for forming a government, the opposition, the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and two accountability tools.
questions.a: Many parties represent diverse regional, ideological and socio-cultural interests, so people choose among them. The party or coalition with more than 50 per cent of seats forms the government, and the largest opposing group becomes the opposition, which questions it. Parties work within the rules of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Tools such as Question Hour and the RTI Act (or audits by the CAG) let citizens and members check the government's work. Together they mean the government can be voted out and questioned.
s: Multi-party system and diversity of interests
More than 50 per cent rule and the opposition
Parties under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Two accountability tools named
Judgement that together they keep government answerable

questions.q:
A gram panchayat reports spending Rs 18 lakh on building a village library. A citizen's Right to Information request shows bills worth only Rs 14.4 lakh. The department promises a reply to her follow-up question in 30 days. A neighbour urges her to file a Public Interest Litigation at once, but others say the courts will want records first.
(a) Which Act did the citizen use to get the figures?
(b) How much money is unaccounted for, and what percentage of the reported spending is it?
(c) Should she file the Public Interest Litigation now or wait for the reply? Give a decision, with one gain and one risk of your choice, and name one accountability body from the chapter that could examine the accounts.
questions.a: (a) The Right to Information Act, 2005. (b) 18 - 14.4 = Rs 3.6 lakh, which is 20 per cent of 18 lakh. (c) Either choice: file now because a PIL enforces public interest and delay may allow records to change, but the court may want evidence; wait 30 days to gather evidence, but delay may weaken the case. Bodies such as the CAG, CIC, Lokpal or CVC may examine the accounts.
s: (a) The RTI Act, 2005
(b) Rs 3.6 lakh and 20 per cent
(c) A decision with a gain, a risk and one named accountability body

questions.q:
In an election to a 230-seat state assembly, Party A won 104 seats, Party B 96, Party C 18 and independents and others 12. Neither of the two larger parties has the numbers to govern alone. Party C's leader must decide whether to support A or B.
(a) How many seats does a party or coalition need to form the government, and does A or B have it alone?
(b) Work out the totals for A with C, and for B with C, and say which can form the government without the independents.
(c) Advise Party C: support A or B, or sit in opposition? Give a decision with the data, and say what the chapter says the largest opposing group is called.
questions.a: (a) More than 50 per cent of 230 means at least 116; A (104) and B (96) fall short. (b) A + C = 122 (enough); B + C = 114 (not enough without the 12 independents; with them 126). (c) Either: join A for a secure 122, but only 6 above the threshold and with a smaller party's influence on policy; or join B and win the 12 independents for 126, harder to arrange. If C stays out, it sits across from the government; the chapter calls the largest opposing group the opposition.
s: (a) 116 seats needed; neither A nor B has it
(b) 122 for A with C; 114 for B with C
(c) A reasoned advice with the figures and the term opposition

questions.q: Members of a dairy cooperative vote on the price at which the society will buy milk, each member having one vote. Which statement from the chapter does this best support?

(b) A fitting example with its bridging role

A combination is acceptable if reasoned.

(c) A choice with a gain and a limit

(b) How much extra does the fee bring in per day and over a 30-day month, and is 31 of 60 a majority?

(b) 800 x (3 - 2) = Rs 800 a day; 800 x 30 = Rs 24,000 a month; 31 is more than half of 60, so a majority. (c) Either: implement, since a majority has decided and the income is Rs 24,000 a month; or discuss further, since 29 members opposed and the cooperative thrives on shared responsibility; reasons required.
s: (a) Cooperatives and community bodies adopt democratic methods
(b) Rs 800 a day, Rs 24,000 a month and 31 is a majority
(c) A reasoned decision weighing the majority against the 29

Reason (R): Social prejudices continue to act as barriers to women's adequate representation in politics.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are stated in the chapter. But the continuing barriers do not explain why the vote came without a struggle; that was because Universal Adult Franchise was extended to all citizens in 1950.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each place or provision with what the chapter says about it.
1. Jethipura Gram Panchayat
2. South Manubankul Gram Panchayat
3. Autonomous District Councils
4. PESA Act, 1996
a. Recognised nationally as a women-friendly panchayat
b. Won the Nanaji Deshmukh Rashtriya Gaurav Gram Sabha Puraskar in 2019
c. Legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs in specific north-eastern regions
d. Makes the Gram Sabha the primary decision-making body in tribal areas of other states
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Jethipura won the 2019 award; South Manubankul is the women-friendly panchayat; ADCs are north-eastern; PESA covers tribal areas in other states.

questions.q: India has about 96.8 crore registered voters and more than 10 lakh polling stations. On average, a station serves fewer than ___ voters.
21 States and 2 Union Territories have 50 per cent reservation for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions. Together that is ___ States and Union Territories.
True or False: Article 243(d) provides not less than one-third reservation for women in every Panchayat, and some States have gone further and provided 50 per cent.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Article 243(d) gives not less than one-third of the directly elected seats to women, and 21 States and 2 Union Territories have provided 50 per cent in their State Panchayati Raj Acts.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: one-third under Article 243(d), and 50 per cent in 21 States and 2 Union Territories

questions.q: A Panchayat has 18 directly elected seats. (a) What is the least number reserved for women under Article 243(d)? (b) How many would be reserved in a State that provides 50 per cent, and how many more is that?
questions.a: (a) One-third of 18 = 6 seats. (b) 50 per cent of 18 = 9 seats, which is 3 more.
s: (a) 6 seats
(b) 9 seats, 3 more

questions.q: (a) In which regions does the chapter say Autonomous District Councils are set up, and what authority do they have? (b) Where does the PESA Act apply, and which body does it empower?
questions.a: (a) Specific north-eastern regions; legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs. (b) Tribal areas in other states; the Gram Sabha as the primary decision-making body.
s: (a) North-eastern regions and legislative and judicial authority
(b) Tribal areas in other states and the Gram Sabha

questions.q: Women gained full voting rights in Britain in 1928 and in the USA in 1920. (a) Which came first and by how many years? (b) Why does the chapter say Indian women did not need a prolonged struggle for the vote, and what barrier does it say remains?
questions.a: (a) The USA, 8 years before Britain. (b) When the Constitution came into force in 1950, Universal Adult Franchise was extended to all citizens, men and women alike. Social prejudices still hinder women's adequate representation in politics.
s: (a) USA first, by 8 years
(b) Franchise given to all in 1950; social prejudices remain a barrier

questions.q: What does 'quorum' mean in a Gram Sabha, and why is it important that Jethipura ensured adequate quorum?
questions.a: Quorum is the presence of the minimum number of members needed to make the proceedings valid. Without it, decisions of the Gram Sabha would not be valid, so ensuring quorum made participation real.
s: Meaning of quorum
Why it matters: valid decisions and real participation

questions.q: Tarun says, 'India's democracy is remarkable not only for its numbers but for its reach: it works in many languages and even in remote places.' Test his statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter gives 96.8 crore registered voters, elections in 22 scheduled languages, symbols so that people who cannot read can vote, and more than a million polling stations, even in mountains, forests, deserts and islands and sometimes for a single voter.
s: Verdict: correct
Numbers: voters, parties or polling stations
Reach: languages, symbols and remote stations

questions.q: Using Jethipura and South Manubankul, show that democracy at the grassroots goes beyond voting. Give three points.
questions.a: Jethipura held Gram Sabhas, Special Gram Sabhas and Mahila Sabhas with participation from marginalised sections; South Manubankul promotes women's participation in decision-making and supports self-help groups and health and sanitation; both show citizens taking part in local self-government, which makes democracy more responsive and inclusive.
s: Jethipura's participation practices
South Manubankul's work for women's participation and welfare
Conclusion: democracy is more responsive and inclusive than voting alone

questions.q: The chapter says the right to vote 'does not automatically ensure equal participation'. Interpret this with two pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Although women have had the vote since 1950, social prejudices still affect their adequate representation in politics. This is why Articles 243(d) and 243(t) reserve not less than one-third of local body seats for women, and some States have gone to 50 per cent.
s: The idea: voting does not guarantee equal participation
Evidence: social prejudices as barriers
Evidence: reservation in local bodies

questions.q: Explain India's three-tier system and the two arrangements for tribal areas, and justify the chapter's statement that the Constitution 'provides a unified national framework that draws its strength from the diverse traditions of every community'.
questions.a: The three tiers are Union, State and Local governments, aiding administrative efficiency and participation. Beyond Panchayati Raj and Municipalities, Autonomous District Councils in specific north-eastern regions have legislative and judicial authority to preserve tribal customs. The PESA Act of 1996 applies to tribal areas in other states and makes the Gram Sabha the primary decision-making body. One national framework accommodates these local forms, so unity draws on diversity.
s: Union, State and Local tiers
Autonomous District Councils and their authority
PESA Act and the Gram Sabha
One national framework holding different arrangements
Justification linking unity with diversity

questions.q: Choose four facts from the chapter's 'Don't miss out' list on India's elections and explain how each shows scale, depth or inclusiveness. Include a calculation of the average number of voters per polling station.
questions.a: 96.8 crore voters show scale; 22 scheduled languages and election symbols show inclusiveness; more than a million polling stations, including remote places, show reach, with an average of about 968 voters per station (96.8 crore divided by 10 lakh); over 2,800 registered parties show diversity of views. An MP representing about 25 lakh people shows the size of representation.
s: Four facts correctly chosen
Each linked to scale, depth or inclusiveness
Average of about 968 voters per polling station

questions.q:
A State is considering raising reservation for women in a 24-seat Panchayat from the constitutional minimum to 50 per cent, as 21 States and 2 Union Territories have done. Some members worry that the change leaves fewer seats for men and that new members lack experience.
(a) Which Article gives the minimum, and how many of the 24 seats does it reserve?
(b) How many seats would women hold at 50 per cent, how many fewer seats would men hold, and by what percentage?
(c) Should the State make the change? Give a decision, using the figures and the chapter's point about women's representation.
questions.a: (a) Article 243(d); one-third of 24 = 8 seats. (b) 12 seats; men's seats fall from 16 to 12, which is 4 fewer, a 25 per cent reduction. (c) Either: adopt, since social prejudices still limit women's representation and many States have done so; or delay, since men lose 25 per cent of seats and training may be needed; a reason from the figures is required.
s: (a) Article 243(d) and 8 seats
(b) 12 seats, 4 fewer for men, 25 per cent
(c) A reasoned decision

questions.q:
Kharpur has 600 adult residents, of whom 270 are women and 130 belong to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. After it started Mahila Sabhas, attendance at Gram Sabhas rose. At the first meeting 120 attended, 30 of them women and 10 from SC/ST. At the third meeting 210 attended, 105 women and 36 from SC/ST. The village can fund only one more step this year.
(a) Name two Jethipura practices that Kharpur's steps echo.
(b) Compare the women's share of attendance at the first and third meetings, and say how the SC/ST share of attendance at the third meeting compares with their share of adults.
(c) Which step would you fund and why: a Special Gram Sabha for SC/ST households, or continuing the Mahila Sabhas?
questions.a: (a) Mahila Sabhas and Special Gram Sabhas, with ensuring adequate quorum. (b) Women: 30/120 = 25 per cent, then 105/210 = 50 per cent. SC/ST: 36/210, about 17 per cent, against about 22 per cent of adults. (c) Either: fund the Special Gram Sabha because SC/ST attendance is still below their share, or continue Mahila Sabhas because the women's share has doubled and benefits compound; a reason from the figures is needed.
s: (a) Two Jethipura practices
(b) 25 to 50 per cent, and about 17 against about 22 per cent
(c) A decision justified with the figures

questions.q: A history club reads that, in a certain period, newspapers had to be cleared before printing, many leaders were arrested and most Fundamental Rights were suspended. Which period of the chapter is this?
questions.a: The Emergency of 1975-77. The chapter says that during the Emergency a majority of Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and numerous leaders and activists were arrested.
o: The Emergency of 1975-77
The drafting by the Constituent Assembly from 1946
The spread of colonial rule by the 19th century
The general elections held after the Emergency in 1977

questions.q: The central government dismisses a State's government and the President takes over its administration. Which Article does the chapter's note link with this action?
questions.a: Article 356, President's Rule. The chapter's note says Articles 352, 356 and 360 deal with National Emergency, President's Rule and Financial Emergency respectively.
o: Article 356, President's Rule
Article 352, National Emergency
Article 360, Financial Emergency
Article 368, amendment of the Constitution

questions.q: A false message about a bridge collapse spreads on social media and two neighbourhoods begin to quarrel. Which warning in the chapter does this illustrate?
questions.a: Misinformation can influence opinion, create confusion and sometimes lead to conflict. The chapter names the spread of fake news through social media as a major concern, saying it can influence public opinion, create confusion and sometimes lead to conflict.
o: Misinformation can influence opinion, create confusion and sometimes lead to conflict
Illiteracy is the only cause of every conflict between neighbourhoods
Social media should never be used by citizens to express opinions
Rumours harm democracy only when they are printed in newspapers

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Emergency.
1. Unemployment, inflation and allegations of misgovernance in the early 1970s led to widespread protests before the Emergency.
2. During the Emergency all Fundamental Rights stayed in force and the press stayed free.
3. The general elections of 1977 returned the ruling government to power.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statement 2 is false: a majority of Fundamental Rights were suspended and the press was censored. Statement 3 is false: the defeat of the ruling government in 1977 showed the strength of Indian democracy.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Damaging public property or spreading misinformation weakens democratic values.
Reason (R): Democracy is reflected in everyday behaviour, decision-making and civic responsibility, not in elections alone.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are stated in the chapter, and the reason explains the assertion: because democracy lives in daily conduct, such actions weaken it.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each description with the item from the chapter.
1. A declaration on the grounds of internal disturbance in June 1975
2. The Article dealing with President's Rule
3. The Article dealing with a Financial Emergency
4. The leader popularly known as Lok Nayak who mobilised students and citizens in Bihar and Gujarat
a. Article 360
b. Jayaprakash Narayan
c. National Emergency, Article 352
d. Article 356
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Article 352 is the National Emergency, Article 356 is President's Rule, Article 360 a Financial Emergency; Jayaprakash Narayan was Lok Nayak.

questions.q: The Constitution came into force in 1950 and the Emergency was imposed in 1975, which is ___ years later.
A student group finds that 12 of the 40 messages in its class chat are false. The share of false messages is ___ per cent.
True or False: The chapter says the defeat of the ruling government in the 1977 elections showed the weakness of Indian democracy.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the defeat of the ruling government demonstrated the strength of Indian democracy and the importance of constitutional safeguards, civil liberties and active citizen participation.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the 1977 result showed the strength and resilience of democracy

questions.q: (a) Name two causes of public dissatisfaction in the early 1970s that the chapter mentions. (b) Who led mass movements that mobilised students and citizens, and in which two States?
questions.a: (a) Any two of rising unemployment, inflation and allegations of misgovernance. (b) Jayaprakash Narayan (Lok Nayak), in Bihar and Gujarat.
s: (a) Two valid causes
(b) Jayaprakash Narayan, Bihar and Gujarat

questions.q: (a) Name two challenges to democracy in India, other than fake news, that the chapter lists. (b) How can gaps in implementing laws and policies affect democracy?
questions.a: (a) Any two of illiteracy, inequality, poverty, regionalism, gender inequality and social discrimination. (b) They may reduce public trust in institutions.
s: (a) Two valid challenges
(b) Reduced public trust in institutions

questions.q: A class group checks 40 messages in its chat and finds 12 false. (a) What percentage is false? (b) Name one step from the chapter's discussion that the group should take when it questions a message's reliability.
questions.a: (a) 12/40 = 30 per cent. (b) Discuss what made the message questionable and why access to accurate and authentic information matters, as in the chapter's group activity.
s: (a) 30 per cent
(b) A valid step: questioning reliability and seeking authentic information

questions.q: Write the three Articles in the chapter's note on Emergency and say what each deals with.
questions.a: Article 352: declaration of National Emergency; Article 356: President's Rule; Article 360: Financial Emergency.
s: Articles with two matched correctly
All three matched correctly

questions.q: Anil says, 'The Emergency shows that democracy in India collapsed completely and never recovered.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the Emergency was lifted in 1977 and general elections were held, and the defeat of the ruling government showed the strength of Indian democracy. The chapter says the period highlighted both the vulnerabilities and the resilience of democratic institutions.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Evidence: Emergency lifted, elections held, ruling government defeated
Vulnerability and resilience both highlighted

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a student counters misinformation in her school, and name two civic responsibilities from the chapter that she shows.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. a student sees a forwarded rumour about a holiday, checks the school notice, tells classmates and does not forward it. Responsibilities: using social media responsibly and being media literate (and respecting others' rights).
s: A believable situation
A first responsibility named
A second responsibility named

questions.q: The chapter says indifference towards public issues can adversely affect the health of a democracy. Interpret this with three points.
questions.a: Democracy requires constant care, awareness and participation from institutions and citizens; if citizens ignore public issues, wrongs go unchecked and decisions are taken without informed opinion; democracy is shown in daily behaviour and civic responsibility, not only in elections.
s: Democracy needs continuous care and participation
Indifference lets problems go unchecked
Democracy lives in everyday behaviour and responsibility

questions.q: Describe the Emergency of 1975-77 in five points: the background, the imposition, its effects, the resistance and its end, and justify the chapter's view that it showed both vulnerability and resilience.
questions.a: Background: unemployment, inflation and allegations of misgovernance led to protests. Imposition: a National Emergency was declared in June 1975 on grounds of internal disturbance. Effects: a majority of Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and leaders and activists were arrested. Resistance: Jayaprakash Narayan led mass movements in Bihar and Gujarat. End: it was lifted in 1977 and elections defeated the ruling government. Vulnerability: institutions were strained; resilience: people used the ballot.
s: Background
Imposition in June 1975 and grounds
Effects on rights, press and leaders
Resistance and its end in 1977
Vulnerability and resilience justified

questions.q: Evaluate the challenges to democracy that the chapter lists and propose how a young citizen can respond to three of them, using the chapter's ideas on being well informed and civic responsibility.
questions.a: The chapter lists illiteracy, misinformation, inequality, poverty, regionalism, gender inequality, social discrimination and gaps in implementing laws. A young citizen can be media literate and stay informed through authentic sources to counter misinformation, avoid damaging public property and follow rules, take part in NSS or NCC and community service, and respect others' rights and diversity. These actions build civic responsibility and strengthen democracy.
s: Challenges listed correctly
Response to misinformation
Response to inequality or discrimination through respecting rights
Response through participation such as NSS or NCC
An overall judgement

questions.q:
A school survey of 50 students found that 35 got news about a local protest mainly from social media. Of those 35, 14 shared a post without checking it. In all, a false claim about the protest reached 28 of the 50 students. The principal can either ban phones on campus or start weekly media-literacy sessions.
(a) Which challenge from the chapter does the false claim illustrate?
(b) What percentage got news from social media, what percentage of them shared without checking, and what percentage did the false claim reach?
(c) Which step would you recommend, and why? Use the chapter, giving one gain and one cost.
questions.a: (a) Misinformation and fake news. (b) 35/50 = 70 per cent; 14/35 = 40 per cent; 28/50 = 56 per cent. (c) Either: media-literacy sessions build the responsible use and media literacy the chapter urges but take time; a ban cuts the spread quickly but limits access to information and free expression and does not teach judgement.
s: (a) Misinformation or fake news
(b) 70, 40 and 56 per cent
(c) A reasoned recommendation with a gain and a cost

questions.q:
A library club debates the Emergency. One member says emergency powers are needed to keep order; another says they endanger democracy. Facts the club gathers: the Emergency was imposed in 1975, 25 years after the Constitution came into force, on grounds of internal disturbance; most Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and leaders were arrested; it was lifted in 1977 and the ruling government lost the elections.
(a) Under which Article is a National Emergency declared, and in which year was this one imposed?
(b) Name two freedoms or practices that were affected.
(c) Take a side in the club's debate. State your position using the facts, and name one safeguard that would reduce the risk of misuse.
questions.a: (a) Article 352; 1975. (b) Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and leaders and activists were arrested. (c) Either side with reasons: order may need special powers for internal disturbance, but suspending rights and censoring the press strained institutions, and the 1977 election showed that the people used the ballot to respond. Safeguards: constitutional safeguards, civil liberties, a free press, courts and active citizens.
s: (a) Article 352 and 1975
(b) Two valid effects
(c) A position with facts and a named safeguard
